units.t: Safety & Survival Shorts. Episode two.
In this episode: Cold water and hypothermia, Severe storms and cyclones and Staying alive on long drives.
Part one. Cold water and hypothermia.
Many people who die in cold water drown before hypothermia ever sets in.
The first minute is the most dangerous, and the instinct to swim hard can be exactly the wrong one.
More than a polar risk.
Hypothermia isn't only for polar explorers.

In Australia, people get into trouble with cold regularly: bushwalkers in Tasmania caught by sudden storms, even in summer, skiers and hikers in the Alps, rock fishers swept into winter seas, and kayakers and boaters who capsize in cold rivers and lakes.
Water is the great accelerator, drawing heat from the body far faster than air at the same temperature.
Wind and wet clothing do something similar on land.
Add rain, tiredness and inadequate clothing, and a person can become dangerously cold on a seemingly mild day, especially in the mountains, where weather can change within an hour.
Cold water shock.
When a person suddenly falls into cold water, the shock on the skin triggers an involuntary gasp, followed by rapid, uncontrollable breathing, a racing heart and a spike in blood pressure.
This cold shock response peaks in the first minute or so.
If your head is underwater during that first gasp, you can inhale water and drown almost immediately, long before the body cools.
The racing heart can also trigger heart problems in people at risk.
That is why many cold water deaths happen close to shore or a boat, and why even strong swimmers can drown quickly after an unexpected fall.
Float first.
The instinct is to thrash and swim hard.
But swimming and panicking during cold shock makes breathing harder to control and raises the risk of inhaling water.
Water safety groups, including Britain's Royal National Lifeboat Institution, now teach: float first.
Lean back, spread your arms and legs, and keep your face out of the water, moving your hands gently if needed, until the gasping and fast breathing settle, typically within a minute or two.
Then you can think clearly: signal for help, grab something that floats, or swim to safety if it's close.
A lifejacket makes all of this far easier.
The 1-10-1 rule of thumb sums up the timing: roughly one minute to control your breathing, ten minutes of meaningful movement, and an hour or more before unconsciousness.
Signs and first aid.
Hypothermia means core temperature has dropped below about 35 degrees Celsius, from a normal of around 37.
Early signs are intense shivering, cold pale skin and fumbling hands.
Then come the 'umbles': stumbling, mumbling, fumbling and grumbling, with slurred speech and slow, confused thinking.
In severe cases shivering stops, a dangerous sign rather than a good one.
Watch each other closely, because judgement fades early.
Call 000 for anything beyond mild hypothermia.
Move them out of wind, rain or water and handle them gently.
Replace wet clothes with dry layers or wrap them in blankets, including head and neck, and insulate from the ground.
If alert, give warm sweet drinks, never alcohol.
Don't rub limbs or use a hot bath.
Start CPR if they stop breathing normally.
Reach or throw.
Each year people drown trying to rescue others, often family members, including children and dogs.
The safest approach is reach or throw, don't go.
Call 000.
Then reach the person from a safe position with a pole, branch, rope or towel, lying down on the bank for balance, or throw something that floats, such as a lifebuoy, an esky, a bodyboard or a ball.
Tell them to float on their back and keep calm.
Only trained rescuers with proper equipment should enter the water, especially if it's cold or fast-flowing.
Prevention is simpler: wear a lifejacket when boating or rock fishing, dress in layers, check the forecast and tell someone where you're going.
The key idea: Hypothermia is an Australian risk too, and water pulls heat from the body far faster than air.
Part two. Severe storms and cyclones.
Every year, wild storms and tropical cyclones tear roofs off, drop trees on cars and cut power to thousands of homes.
Knowing what to do before and during one can keep your family safe.
Storm country.
On a hot spring afternoon in south-east Queensland or western Sydney, towering clouds can drop giant hail, flatten fences and flood streets in under an hour.
Severe thunderstorms happen across most of Australia.
In the tropical north the bigger threat is the tropical cyclone, which forms over warm ocean water.
The cyclone season runs from November to April.
The Bureau of Meteorology rates cyclones from Category 1 to 5, with Category 3 and above called severe.
But the category describes only wind.
A weaker cyclone can still be deadly through flooding rain, which can spread hundreds of kilometres inland, or storm surge.
Cyclones can also strengthen rapidly or change direction, so don't relax at 'only' a low category.
The danger of storm surge.
When a strong cyclone nears a coast, powerful winds push ocean water toward the shore, and the low air pressure at its centre lets the sea bulge upward.
The result is a storm surge: sea level well above normal high tide, topped with large waves.
If it arrives at high tide, it can flood low-lying coastal suburbs, roads and caravan parks.
Around the world, surge has caused many of the deadliest cyclone disasters.
In Australia, authorities may order people in surge zones to evacuate even if their homes are well built, because the threat is water, not wind.
If you live near the coast in cyclone country, find out whether you are in a storm surge zone.
Preparing your home.
Much storm damage comes from flying debris and falling trees.
Before the season, clean gutters and downpipes, trim overhanging branches, use a qualified arborist for large trees, and check the roof.
List loose items such as trampolines, outdoor furniture, bins and pot plants to secure or bring inside when a warning is issued.
In cyclone areas, residents often fit shutters or protect windows, and learn whether their home was built to modern cyclone standards.
Keep your emergency kit stocked, fill vehicles with fuel, and charge phones and power banks when a warning comes.
Park cars under cover or away from trees if hail is forecast.
For storm damage that is not life-threatening, call the SES on 132 500.
Sheltering safely.
In a severe storm or cyclone, the safest place is usually indoors in the strongest part of the building, often a small internal room such as a bathroom, laundry or hallway, away from windows.
If the building breaks up, protect yourself under a sturdy table or mattress.
In a cyclone, be wary of the calm eye: the wind drops and the sky may clear, then the winds return, often from the opposite direction and just as strong.
Stay in until authorities say it has passed.
Lightning can strike many kilometres from the rain, so if you can hear thunder, you are in range.
Go indoors or into a hard-topped car, and avoid open ground, water and isolated trees.
It is safe to touch a lightning victim; call 000 and start CPR if they aren't breathing normally.
After the storm.
The clean-up brings its own risks.
Always assume fallen power lines are live.
Stay well clear, at least 8 metres according to many electricity networks, and remember that water, fences and wet ground near a line can be electrified too.
Report them to your electricity distributor, or call Triple Zero, 000, if there is immediate danger.
Don't enter badly damaged buildings, and watch for broken glass, exposed nails and asbestos in older homes.
Avoid driving through floodwater or under damaged trees.
Chainsaw and ladder injuries are common after storms, so be cautious or leave big jobs to professionals and the SES.
Photograph damage before clearing it, for insurance.
This is general information; follow official advice for your area.
The key idea: Australia faces severe thunderstorms and tropical cyclones, and cyclone categories describe wind only, not total danger.
Part three. Staying alive on long drives.
Australia's long, empty roads are beautiful, but fatigue, wildlife and remote breakdowns catch out even experienced drivers.
Here is how to make every road trip end safely.
The hypnotic road.
There is something hypnotic about a long Australian highway: straight bitumen, red dirt, a horizon that never gets closer.
That is part of the danger.
Most Australians live in cities, yet a large share of road deaths happen on rural and regional roads, often in single-vehicle crashes where a car leaves the road or hits a tree.
Speeds are higher, roads may be narrow or unsealed, and help can be hours away.
Road safety campaigns talk about the 'fatal five': speeding, drink and drug driving, not wearing a seatbelt, fatigue and distraction.
On long drives the last two matter most, because they creep up on people who felt fine when they set out.
Fatigue and microsleeps.
Being awake for a long time impairs reactions and judgement in a way research has compared to having alcohol in your blood.
The scariest part is the microsleep: a few seconds when your brain switches off, often without you realising.
At 100 kilometres per hour a car covers nearly 28 metres every second, so a four-second microsleep carries you well over 100 metres with nobody in control.
Warning signs include yawning, heavy eyes, drifting in your lane, missing signs and not remembering the last few kilometres.
Opening the window or turning up the music does not fix tiredness.
The only real cure is sleep, so pull over somewhere safe for a rest or a power nap.
Planning to beat fatigue.
Fatigue is far easier to prevent than to fight.
Start a long drive well rested, and avoid setting out after a full day of work or when your body normally sleeps, such as late at night and in the mid-afternoon slump.
Road safety agencies commonly recommend a break of at least 15 minutes every two hours.
Get out, walk around, and have a drink and a snack.
Look for Driver Reviver sites, which often operate on major highways in holiday periods and offer free tea, coffee and a chat.
If you can, share the driving with another licensed driver.
Be honest about how far you can go.
An extra night in a motel is a small price compared with the cost of a crash.
Animals, trains and gravel.
Kangaroos, wallabies, wombats, emus and livestock are a real hazard, especially at dawn, dusk and night.
Slow down where wildlife signs appear and scan the verges for eyes reflecting your headlights.
If an animal jumps out, brake firmly in a straight line.
Many serious crashes happen when drivers swerve, lose control and hit a tree or oncoming vehicle.
Kangaroos can change direction suddenly, and where there is one there are often more.
Road trains, trucks towing several trailers, can stretch beyond 50 metres.
Pass only with a long, clear view ahead.
If one approaches on a narrow road, slow down and move left.
On gravel, drive slower, avoid harsh braking and steering, and keep your headlights on in dust.
Check road conditions first, as roads may close after rain.
Remote breakdowns and help.
Before heading remote, tell someone your route and arrival time.
Carry far more water than you think you need, plus food, a first aid kit, a spare tyre and tools.
Mobile coverage vanishes across much of Australia, so many travellers carry a satellite device or personal locator beacon.
If you break down, stay with your vehicle.
It is far easier for searchers to spot than a person, and it gives shade.
People have died walking away in extreme heat.
After a crash, get clear of traffic and turn on your hazard lights.
Call Triple Zero, 000, if someone is hurt or trapped, a vehicle is on fire or the road is blocked.
The free Emergency+ app shows your GPS location to read to the operator.
A first aid course will prepare you to help.
The key idea: Country roads carry a disproportionate share of Australia's road deaths, and fatigue and distraction are the quiet killers on long drives.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why does cold water chill the body so much faster than air?
Answer. It draws heat from the body far faster than air.
Question two. What does a cyclone's category describe?
Answer. Wind strength only.
Question three. Why are long country drives especially risky?
Answer. Higher speeds, fatigue and help being far away.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
